title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend

reading.body:
This is a case of an authorised operator turning a deployed system against its intended purpose. The license plate readers were installed for police work, and the chief had legitimate access to them, so no access control was defeated and no outsider broke in. The failure sits at the point of use, where a person with valid credentials directed a surveillance tool at a private target rather than a police matter.

Nothing in the reporting describes a technical safeguard that would have stopped the queries as they were made. Catching it would have required looking at the pattern afterwards, meaning an audit of who searched for whom and how often, and a review that flagged repeated lookups connected to someone with a personal tie to the officer. The conduct was reportedly noticed through other means, including his own admission and the certification process.

The certification order is a finding by a state body, not a criminal verdict, and no criminal outcome is reported here. The headline gives one number of searches and the summary gives another, so the exact count is not settled by the material available. The order records that jealousy influenced his conduct, which is an admission about his state of mind, not a finding about what he intended the system to do.

reports.title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend

summary: From June to October 2023, Sedgwick, Kansas, Police Chief Lee Nygaard reportedly used Flock Safety license-plate readers 228 times to check the whereabouts of his ex-girlfriend and her new boyfriend, according to a Kansas certification order. The order said Nygaard also followed them in a police vehicle and admitted that jealousy influenced his conduct. He resigned in October 2023 and later lost his police certification.
